name: Elena Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy for a pharmacy wholesaler. We supply about three hundred chemists with over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, plasters, baby products. I handle the vitamins and first aid range. My day is reading the demand report, placing orders with manufacturers, and handling shortages, because when a cough syrup goes short in winter, every chemist rings us at once.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the puzzle of a shortage, finding an alternative supplier and getting it on the shelves before the panic. What's hard is the paperwork, batch numbers and expiry dates and recalls. I've started using an AI tool now and then to compare supplier price lists, but I still check it, because a mistake in my world can end up in someone's medicine cabinet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds believable. It'd tidy up some paperwork and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool that got oversold, and that we should use it where it's safe and leave the rest. Probably not much online; I don't post a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved and fairly secure. Pharmacy supply is regulated and people want a human checking it. Tomas, my partner, is a civil engineer, so between us we're steady, and we've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and keep using the price-list tool. We'd carry on saving for a house deposit, maybe in two years. And I'd ask my manager about the senior buyer post that's opening next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the hype, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything at all that would worry you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company's owned by a bigger group and they keep merging departments. That's not AI, that's just business, but it means I keep my head down and do good work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the senior buyer post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for it. Ten percent more pay and I'd run the shortage desk. I've covered it twice when my colleague was off, so I know I can.

say: AI is a **useful tool** that got oversold.
Use it where it's **safe** and leave the rest alone.
think: Pharmacy supply is **regulated**, and people want a human checking it.
With Tomas's **engineering pay**, we're steady with four months saved.
do: Keep using the **price-list tool** and checking it.
Keep saving for a **house deposit** in about two years.
Apply for the **senior buyer** post next spring.
S0.quote: Pharmacy supply is regulated and people want a human checking it.
fieldNote: Elena feels **secure**: regulated work and a two-income household.
Her quiet risk is **corporate merging**, which she treats as normal business.
She's ready to **step up** to senior buyer.

steps.text: Apply for the senior buyer post next spring
Keep saving for a house deposit within two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's my job on the list. Buying, checking, planning. Every word.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change how we work and we'd better be sensible about it. At work I'd suggest we test the tools on the easy ranges first, like plasters, not medicines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry about the senior post. If AI does most of the ordering, they won't need a shortage desk with three people. My job could shrink to checking the machine's work, with fewer of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start using the AI tools properly, every day, once I saw a colleague get good results. I'd do a short course on pharmacy regulations and quality checks, because checking is the part that'll stay longest. And we'd put the house deposit on hold for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but I'd be watching every team meeting for signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for a colleague. Who?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planner, who tries everything first. If the planner's numbers come out better with AI, I'll copy the setup. I don't need to be first with the AI tools, I just can't be last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas my job's on the line more than his for now. Engineers still have to sign drawings and stand on site. We'd agree to keep the deposit in the bank, not spend it.

say: This will change how we work, so we should be **sensible** about it.
Test the tools on easy ranges like **plasters**, not medicines.
think: The **senior post** might vanish if AI runs ordering.
My job could shrink to **checking the machine's** work, with fewer of us.
do: Use the AI tools **every day** once a colleague proves them.
Take a short course in **regulations and quality** checks.
Put the **house deposit** on hold for a year.
feel: **Anxious**, watching every team meeting for signs.
S1.quote: I don't need to be first with the AI tools, I just can't be last.
fieldNote: Elena sees her **whole role** in the card and shifts to worry.
She'd follow a **trusted colleague** into the tools, a steady person's move.
She bets on **quality checking** as the part of the job that lasts.

steps.text: Copy the planner's AI ordering setup once it proves itself
Take a short course in pharmacy regulations and quality checks
Hold the house deposit in the bank for a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a shock. My whole department would be gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, fast, especially for medicines. A human should have to sign off on anything that goes into a pharmacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the buying job ends. Even the checking could be done by AI by 2028. The only hands-on bit is visiting the warehouse when there's a recall, and robots come for that in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at becoming a pharmacy technician, which is hands-on and regulated, and takes about two years to train. I'd stop all big spending and keep our savings ready. We'd lean on Tomas's salary, and probably move to a smaller flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the job I built just evaporated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Tomas's job safe in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. A lot of his design work is thinking work. But someone still has to be on site and sign off, so he'd last longer than me. We'd be one income for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car. We'd go back to one car and the bus. Then eating out. The savings stay untouched as long as possible.

say: We need **rules fast**, especially for medicines.
A **human should sign off** on anything that goes into a pharmacy.
think: The **buying job ends**; even checking could be done by AI by 2028.
Recall visits are my only **hands-on** work, and robots reach those by 2031.
do: Train as a **pharmacy technician**, about two years.
Sell the **second car** and cut eating out.
Live on **Tomas's salary** and move to a smaller flat.
S2.quote: A human should have to sign off on anything that goes into a pharmacy.
fieldNote: Elena expects her **whole department** to go in two years.
Her pivot to **pharmacy technician** keeps her in a regulated, hands-on field.
Tomas's **longer-lasting job** becomes the household's anchor.

steps.text: Sell the second car and stop eating out
Move to a smaller flat on Tomas's salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Still fast, but I could see it coming and get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to train people properly and keep medicines safe. I'd back sensible rules from whoever proposed them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the first two years to get good with the AI tools and keep my job. Then I'd train as a pharmacy technician on the side, so I'm ready before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools daily from year one. I'd start part-time technician training in year two. We'd still save for a house, but a cheaper one, and I'd keep six months in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a plan, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still buy a house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one. I'd rather own something than rent when everything's moving. But nothing with a big mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older buyers who've done it for twenty years. They know every manufacturer but they hate screens. I'd offer to show them the tools, but I can't make them learn.

say: We have time to **train people** properly and keep medicines safe.
I'd back **sensible rules** from whoever proposed them.
think: I'd get good with **AI tools** for two years to keep my job.
Then I'd train as a **pharmacy technician** before 2031.
do: Use the AI tools **daily** from year one.
Start **part-time technician** training in year two.
Buy a **cheaper house** and keep six months saved.
S3.quote: I'd rather own something than rent when everything's moving. But nothing with a big mortgage.
fieldNote: Five years lets Elena run a **two-step plan**: tools first, then retraining.
She still wants a **small house**, a centre person's cautious hedge.
She worries about **older colleagues** who resist screens.

steps.text: Use the AI ordering tools daily from year one
Start part-time pharmacy technician training in year two
Buy a cheaper house while keeping six months saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's time for a whole new plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's manageable with good planning, and that we shouldn't panic when there's a decade to prepare. I'd tell friends to start thinking about their next step now, while it's cheap to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be in a different role by 2036 anyway. Maybe running quality and recalls, or as a pharmacy technician. I'd have time to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep buying and use the tools as they come in. We'd buy the house in two years as planned. I'd start technician training around year four or five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but not scared. It feels like something I can steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you trust yourself to start in year four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly. I'd write it down and tell Tomas, so he'd nag me. I'm steady, not lazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would kids come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Ten years is a long time, and we'd want a family in that window. That's one reason the house matters.

say: We **shouldn't panic** when there's a decade to prepare.
Friends should plan their **next step** now, while change is cheap.
think: I'd be in a **different role** by 2036 anyway.
Quality and recalls or **pharmacy technician** work are my likely paths.
do: Keep buying and use **tools as they come**.
Buy the **house in two years** as planned.
Start **technician training** around year four or five.
feel: It feels like something I can **steer**.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time, and we'd want a family in that window.
fieldNote: Elena treats ten years as **ordinary career planning**.
The house and **future children** shape her timing.
She uses Tomas as an **accountability partner** for retraining.

steps.text: Keep buying and adopt the tools as they arrive
Buy the house within two years as planned
Start pharmacy technician training around year four

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My department would be gone before I could train for anything. What would help is funded retraining for regulated hands-on roles, and rules that keep a human signing off on medicines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about safety. Everyone talks about jobs, but if a machine orders the wrong batch of medicine, who's responsible?

headlineQuote: If a machine orders the wrong batch of medicine, who's responsible?
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old buyer** of vitamins and first aid at a pharmacy wholesaler, living with Tomas, an engineer.
She uses AI **now and then** and follows a trusted colleague before committing.
She's **pragmatic** and wants rules to keep medicines safe.
She's calm in the plateau, **alarmed** in fast AGI, uneasy with ten years.
Her landing plan is **pharmacy technician** work, regulated and hands-on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with her department gone before she can retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Rules keeping a **human sign-off** on medicines.
